title: Hitman: Codename 47
text: Hitman is a staple franchise of the IO Interactive company and was distributed by Eidos, the same company that distributed the first two waves of the Tomb Raider franchise. The game centers around a genetically engineered clone who goes by no name other than "47" escapes from an asylum after going through various tests in both combat and weapon skills. A year later 47 was recruited by the ICA(International Contract Agency) a government division that specializes in assassinations, espionage, & terrorism. Agent 47 goes on global missions to assassinated various crime lords, drug dealers, weapon smugglers, thugs, terrorists, etc. Upon his travels, 47 notices that there's a connection between the targets he's executed and is willing to piece the puzzle together to find out who they all work for. The first entry in the series has it's share of clunky controls, occasional glitches, and situations that defy logic. These isssues, I can look past as the game does offer a challenge and fun factor. After the release of this game, Agent 47 would soon be ranked as a favorite anti hero for games. His cross of Vin Diesel and Golgo 13 gives him an iconic look along with situations and moments that will remind you of Terminator, Nikita, Scarface, and Leon the Professional. This was the first game to use a fully composed orchestra, the first to use the rag doll function(whenever you drag a corpse is moves like a doll), and the earliest use of the cloth function on the character's clothing. Keep in mind that the later games do get better, as at times this game can be frustrating with no mid level saving,minimum health meter, and poor functionality of disguises. But again this is only the first game, so give it some mercy. Anyways if you like playing a third person shooter where you have various options to kill a target, choices of prefered weapons to use on the missions, and various disguises to put on will make this game worth your while.

title: Hitman: Codename 47
text: Hitman: Codename 47 started one of the best stealth franchises ever developed. For a 2000 game it had high complexity, but also a quite high difficulty curve. I remember hating the entire series because when I was younger, I didn't even manage to complete the first mission with a Silent Assassin rating after countless tries. Oh the memories. Looking back at the game now, it still is astonishing how many of the key elements of the Hitman franchise already existed in the first game and how many of those still successfully survived until this very day. Proof for good game design, if I ever saw any. I still had fun running through this game 17 years later, but one should never forget that it is 17 years old: Controls are unwieldy, enemy AI and detection makes zero sense whatsoever and the game feels quite 'clunky' at times. All the same, Hitman: Codename 47 is a milestone of gaming history.

title: Home
text: The protagonist wakes in a strange home with no recollection of what brought him there - but a few encounters with dead bodies, bloodstains, and abandoned weapons make it clear that the circumstances are grim. You move this highly pixelated character through highly pixelated 2D environments, interacting with doors, ladders, and objects as you try to piece together a growing mystery. The game is a very short, very inexpensive experiment that is intriguing in the way it builds tension only to leave you with more questions than answers. You might return to it multiple times hoping to fill in the gaps, but ultimately realize that the game wasn't really telling you a complete story. is as much a choose your own adventure novel as a game, but the story it tells is disturbing and unique enough to hold interest despite limited interactivity. Pick up a knife, or leave it be. Watch a videotape, or let well enough alone. It's not always clear what impact these decisions might have at the time, and in fact, it may not be any clearer what the impact was once you finish. may not feature enough actual game for some players, but has successfully made a sophisticated, horrifying story. text: I'm a sucker for atmospheric suspense, and this game has it in spades. I don't think it will convert anyone who isn't a fan of the genre, but those who have an interest will find a lot to like. It's worth noting that the game is not very long (around an hour to play through), but I found it very satisfying and worth my money. Pros: Great atmosphere - The game makes good use of the pixel art style, and the sound design is excellent. Narrative crafting - The core game mechanic is that the choices you make alter the backstory. Gives a real sense that your choices matter. Strong writing - Not great writing, but no false steps that took me out of the experience. Cons: Limited Replayability - Though you can play through with alternate choices to see different takes on the story, I found I'd had enough after the second playthrough.

title: Home
text: Ever been to the movies, to watch something you normally wouldn't watch, and at the end said "Hold up, I need to gather my thoughts."? Home is an open ended game that, in all aspects, works like a movie. Gameplay seems to be just a linear exploration and interacting with stuff that gets highlighted. You are then prompted for your thoughts on some interactions. You say whatever you want/think about it from the given options. You basically are fed ambiguous information that your mind tries to decrypt. You always have the same basic path to reach the same end-point. And you always have to make one fundamental choice. Without giving any spoiler, since this game is all about the experience, the ending ruins everything. Not because there is an ending, but because basically you answer some relevant questions and are given an akward explanation that goes with whatever you answered. This is crucially flawed, in my opinion, since "every run will be different", but not by much: there's one critical event at the very end that is foreshadowed throught the irreversible middle-sections that the narrator uses to conveniently sum up the important things you perceived, and the rest is pretty much meaningless. The ambience is pretty much all this game has going in its favour. Should you pick up the knife on the floor, covered with what appears to be blood? It depends on your current view about yourself, a guy that seems to know very little about himself. Does freeing the rat from the rat trap in any way change the outcome of it all? I don't know, and I don't care enough to find out. Is it that the list of girls you run into twice mean that you murdered them? You can see where this is going. You, the player, are the one that is putting meaning into the things you find. The one and only thing I was curious about while playing the game was , but even that isn't enough to make me want to go through playing the game again. The reason I have 2.1 hours on record is also because when I first played the game there was no autosave mechanism implemented and had to quit at about 40 minutes in because of stuff in the real world; the game is that short. Also, I don't consider this to be a major spoiler, but Home is absolutely titled the way it is because a) you find yourself initially in someone else's, and b) you end the game at yours. The game has a metascore of 69 out of 100: I guess it's a fair value. I personally got Home at a big discount, and I'd advise you to do the same if you really want to play it. If you want something with a little more gameplay and can handle the horror genre, try Lone Survivor since it's an overall better investment.

title: Home
text: Home is a 2D side scrolling mystery story based game. You'll walk left and right, open doors and find clues. The clues help you find out why you woke up in someone else's house and what has happened to your wife Rachel. Objects you can interact with will have an outline when you walk next to them. You will collect items, but have no inventory. The game spans a few locations and each location has several different rooms. Two houses, woods, a sewer system and a factory. There are locked doors and you'll need to find keys, hairpins and other ways to open them. After each location, the character will reference objects that you found and ponder what they could mean. The art style is very pixelated for better or worse. It doesn't feel too detailed. The only animation is the character's walk animation. Everything else is a static object. The game is very story based and you will be reading a lot. My only problem with the dialog is that it has its own screen. It takes me out of the game when it has its own screen. As game calling itself horror, it is all at night and your character is carrying a lantern. While you come across pixelated horror such as dead night watchmen and read about it, there is no threat. So its not scary. Nothing is out to get you. There is no pressure. As you search through the locations you'll tackle a few light puzzles to progress forward. You'll find dead bodies and read through text about how rancid trash is and some back story about your character. Even with no map, I don't feel like I ever got lost. Most things you find, you get a choice to take it or not. Find a bloody knife, do you take it or leave it? Normally the choice would be laughable. Of course people want to take it. Well everything you take leads up to something and what you take and the story molds itself nicely to what you have and don't have. That's really what this game excels at, an interactive story that molds itself to your choices. Do you uncover a pair of bodies? Do you take a video tape that is potential evidence? Do you read a letter that you find hanging out of a mailbox? Did you find a list of names or not? Home can be played in an hour or so. My second time through I speed ran it in about 20 minutes. There are many different endings depending on the choices you made. Even with different endings, I don't feel like the game is worth replaying. Its over too quick to give impact to any ending. The game feels like there wasn't much effort put in. Everything is text, no real animation. I'm reading emotions rather than seeing the graphics convey the emotions. Television and video games are visual mediums. I should be seeing things, not reading them. I wouldn't be so harsh on the text if it didn't have its own dedicated screen to take me out of the game.

title: Home
text: I usually give games a few days of play before reviewing them. But I think I've seen enough. Home is an 8-bit looking pixel horror adventure game. It pretty much operates like all the old point and click acventures of old. It tells you on boot to turn out all the lights...and put on headphones. Fair enough. I do agree that games which favor spookiness need to be played in a certain way...at a certain time. This one does it so it can clip-clop loud footsteps and doorcreaks at you. Pretty much insistently and annoyingly. It does so so in-your-face that when you click on a door to move through it it shows you a pixelated door opening in full screen with accompanying LOUD door creak. Same with going up and down stairs. That...really...makes me laugh after awhile. But not funny haha. Funny as in...I can't believe they thought this worked. You start off in mystery house during a rainstorm without knowing how you got there. You do the same point and click searching and picking up and using things you always do in these. But nothing happens. Nothing is scary. In the occasional room there is a noise, a slamming, mysterious whisper but at this point I don't really read it as having anything to do with the story or the game itself. But more oooooo dev is trying to scare me with spooky sounds. Not thrilled by the puzzles thus far. And really not thrilled that once I got past a certain part, it won't let me go back and check out a door that I missed. Isn't a big point of adventure games that they are freeflowing? YOu can go visit and explore places? Read their descriptions? Enjoy the atmosphere? Well here is another fact of this game. It has laughable bugs. When I got bored I saved the game. WHen I started it up again and hit continue...TWO of me were on the screen. That's right. My character (the protagonist) is on the screen normally but since I restarted it had two copies of it. Once I went into the next room it went away. So like I already was thinking this didn't have someone helping with content. NOw I know it didn't have anyone testing it either. The story is what could have saved this. Events could have saved this. But neither have occurred. Edit: I've now finished the game...one run thru of it. I have to correct myself. The save bug does NOT go away. It is revealed when you use the mouse to move. You will always have two of yourself walking around the room once you restart. Now let's talk about the writing. Let's just drop this logic problem...At the beginning...you are trying to get out of the house. You come to a front door and...you can't leave...because there is furniture stacked in front of it! Why can't you just move the furniture like everyone else would do? There are lots of things like this. Also this game is written as if it was written in the past. This gimmick does not work. At all. It makes the game seems wishy washy. Makes it seem like nothing you do matters and that you aren't really trying to solve anything. Which I guess you aren't. It is telling the story and whatever you do is fine. That's the story. So there is no emotional impact for anything at all since you take it where you want. Someone also mentioned the achievements. Yes...the achievements also make no sense. And many bits at the end don't really make sense either. This needed so much more polish. It really is a grind.

title: Home
text: I bought Home at the same time I bought Lone Survivor when they were both on sale. Lone Survivor was good, Home not so much. Once you start Home, the game informs you that it is best played in a dark room while wearing headphones and that it should only take an hour or so to beat. Suitably prepared for jump scares after the recomendation to use headphones, I dawned them and turned off the lights. You begin by waking up in a strage house with no memory of the events prior to falling asleep, so far so standard. After stumbling around the house looking at things, the game's first piece of horror comes in the form of a door slamming somewhere in the house. This did startle me and now made me feel unsafe in what I had hought was an empty house. For about the next twenty minutes the game makes me feel tense. The sudden noises and clostrophobic amount of light you have to see by do well to create a sense of atmosphere and tension. However, this didn't last. Around the thrid time hearing a noise I was on the edge of my seat; expecting something to leap out and tear my face off any second. By the eigth time I heard a noise, I realized 'any second' wasn't ever going to come. All too soon I realized that all the game had up its sleeve were noises, creating the illusion of being stalked by something that never shows up. Indeed nothing much happens at all in this game. Starting from the most generic opening, the game never solidifies. You are searching for a way out of you initial location and get home to your wife, stumbling through the wake of some monster or killer that is presumably present. Along the way you come across a bunch of seemingly unconnected murder victims and personal effects of your wife, all of it remaining a huge mystery up until the end. But instead of there actually being any form of resolution the game down right expects you to choose your twist ending; blatantly asking you which twist is the one that happens. Then you must choose how you rationalize the events with the ending you chose. This ends up creating a jumbled mess of meaningless atempts at symbolism and rendering pointless any build-up you might have felt as you are forced to choose the meaning behind every mystery in the game. Admittedly I missed one or two things. I never found out what was on the tape and I missed one or two rooms in the factory because I didn't realize the door that required a key card would lock behind me and force me to exit the level. But I don't feel like any of that would have helped. Even if the game weren't a pile of random environments and situations that might be considered spooky, anything they might have lended to the plot would all be rendered meaningless by choosing your ending anyway. All in all, both the horror and the story held no weight and left me feeling let down.

title: Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number
text: I really, really like Hotline Miami. I really, really like Hotline Miami 2. However, a lot of fans of the first Hotline Miami felt very alienated by this game. First of all, if you haven't played the first Hotline Miami, go for that one first. Most people agree that game is fantastic, and helps make sense of this game. One aspect that was drastically changed is the focus on story. Hotline Miami 2 is far more narratively driven than the first game. Furthermore, the game, instead of following one characters story, it follows several. There are far more cutscenes than in the first game. Another aspect is the change in level design. Level design is far more open, and far more punishing. There are a lot more long hallways with glass windows. This means that players have to take different routes than they might in the first game. Finally, combat was changed a little. In tandem with the level design, the game feels far more gun based than the previous installment. Also, character variation is a more limited, due partially to the story's style. I personally adored this game. I thought the storytelling style was very engaging and interesting. I felt that the combat still flowed and felt great. I felt that the level design, while different, was still clearly masterful. But you might not. So take that all into account when buying this game.

title: Hyper Light Drifter
text: Hyper Light Drifter is an incredibly atmospheric journey in a mysterious alien world. The soundtrack conveys the mood perfectly and really fits in with the overall theme of the game. HLD has a bit of a legend of Zelda feel to it as you are free to go wherever you want and the game does not hold your hand with waypoints. The story is told entirely through images and you must use your imagination to try and interpret what is happening. Exploring the world is very fun as there are secrets everywhere, including new guns and outfits which offer a variety of effects. The combat is fast paced and fluid as the Drifter can chain quick dashes, slash to reflect enemy projectiles, and return fire with 1 of 6 unique guns. Slashing enemies refills your ammo and using all of these abilities together makes for an incredibly satisfying experience. There are also a few challenge modes like boss rush, hoarde mode, and NG+ for added replayability. There is even local co-op which works quite well. If you are looking for an adventure in a stunning environment with tight controls I highly recommend Hyper Light Drifter.

title: Hyper Light Drifter
text: I probably should have played the game longer to unlock its secrets and see why everyone loves it so much, but since it was part of a humble bundle I decided against that. Played it for about 40 minutes and nothing in the game convinced me. First I had to watch a pretty irritating intro sequence that didn't really help set the mood or anything. NPCs in the gameworld don't talk, but just display some pictures. The "map", such as it is, is annoying to navigate. Figuring out what to do next is possible, but everything is kinda murky. It tries to be dark soulsy in this aspect I guess without achieving it. At least you can teleport on the map. I also unlocked something, but I have no idea what it does...there are no descriptive texts in the game that I could find. There is no real tutorial and navigating the game map is a chore imho. Instead I was looking forward to the combat system, until I learned that this basically consists of one attack, a dodge and a gun with limited ammo that can be recharged by hitting things. Enemies sometimes appear out of nowhere to hit you, sometimes they're not hit, despite clearly being in the hit zone, etc. It wasn't totally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, but after fighting 6 or so different enemies and employing the same tactics to dispatch them it already got old...hit, evade, hit is pretty much the only thing to do. When you die you respawn at the start of the "map" with all enemies respawned. That's ok. Graphically the game's pixel art looks somehow a lot better in the screenshots than it does in game, which was a sore disappointment, just like the soundtrack, which is neither energetic, nor haunting, nothing. It's just some bad beats that don't complement the game imho. Maybe if the game made it clearer from the start what you're expected to do and in what ways you can improve your character, your move set, etc. then I would have liked it more. As is evidence, many people DO like the game though. These are just my thoughts.
